how_its_made:
STACK
pnpm workspace. TypeScript for the app, SDK, CLI, MCP server and the CRE
workflow; Solidity + Foundry for contracts; Next.js 16 (App Router) for the
interface; viem for all chain access; zod for the typed domain model.

THE EVALUATOR IS THE SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH
`packages/domain` holds one pure function, `evaluateSettlement`, that turns a
private policy plus a live ERP delivery record into a payable amount and a
reason code. It never signs, never authorises a transfer, and has no partial-pay
branch — every invariant violation returns eligible=false with payableAmount=0.
The real Chainlink CRE `handlerInTee` path and the local adapter both reach it
through the identical `runEvaluation` orchestration, so evaluation is
bit-for-bit the same in simulation and in the confidential runtime. The
confidentiality boundary is purely a property of which dependencies were
injected, not a branch inside the logic.

CONTRACTS AND THE KEY DESIGN DECISION
PolicyEpochRegistry (EIP-712 approvals, monotonic epochs), AmendmentEscrow
(prefunded, capped, atomic settle-and-transfer, reentrancy-guarded) and
ReceiptConsumer (the only path into the escrow).

The decision that makes the whole thing work is what `economicEventId` is
derived from: keccak256 over (source tenant, PO id, delivery line id) and
nothing else. It carries no epoch. That is what makes "a new amendment cannot
re-pay an old delivery" an identity property rather than a bookkeeping rule.
The escrow also re-derives beneficiary, cap and revocation live from the
registry rather than trusting the report for anything but amount and event
identity, so a tampered report cannot redirect funds.

CHAINLINK CRE (primary)
The workflow is written against the real `@chainlink/cre-sdk`: `cre.handlerInTee`
for the confidential handler, `runtime.getSecret` for policy material the Vault
DON releases only into an attested enclave, and the confidential-HTTP capability
for the ERP read (the CRE WASM sandbox has no fetch/fs/crypto, so policy secrecy
is CRE's provisioning guarantee, not something we re-implement). The confidential
verdict is a necessary input to settlement, not decoration on top of it.

Honestly: Confidential Workflows is invite-only private beta, so we have NOT run
a live TEE execution. Local simulation is labelled "local adapter" everywhere it
appears — in the UI's runtime panel, in the logs, in the docs. Simulation is
evidence of simulation; we never call it attestation.

PRIVY (secondary)
Research surfaced that `@privy-io/server-auth` is deprecated, so the server
adapter is built against `@privy-io/node` instead. We build real Privy Policy
documents that allowlist exactly two destinations on one chain — the settlement
token and the escrow — and nothing else.

The notable piece: we also wrote a local evaluator implementing Privy's
documented default-deny semantics ("a request satisfying no rule is DENIED"), and
it consumes the exact same policy object that gets registered with Privy when
credentials are present. So the credential-free path enforces the identical
document rather than mocking it away. The app shows a real ALLOW (fund escrow)
and a real DENY (pay the supplier directly, bypassing escrow) with the
per-condition check that decided each — and the denied action never reaches a
signing key.

FRAPPE / ERPNEXT
One `fetch`-based REST client against the documented `/api/resource/:doctype`
contract with token auth. It runs unmodified against a live tenant or the
bundled fixture. The settlement report commits to the document's `modified`
stamp, so an ERP rollback to an older revision cannot be silently replayed as a
fresh confirmation.

THE HACKY BIT WORTH MENTIONING
The web app is not a wireframe over a documented flow. On first request the
server spawns a real anvil devnet, deploys PolicyEpochRegistry, AmendmentEscrow,
ReceiptConsumer and a test token from the project's OWN compiled Foundry
artifacts, and binds a Frappe-shaped fixture server. Every button then drives
that for real: real EIP-712 signatures, real ERC-20 transfers, real reverts. If
Foundry is missing the app says so instead of pretending to work.

Consequence: a revert raised inside the escrow surfaces through the consumer as
a bare 4-byte selector, because the consumer's ABI doesn't declare the escrow's
errors. So we walk the viem error chain for revert data and decode it against
all four contract ABIs — a duplicate settlement reads as
`EventAlreadyConsumed(0xfb38…)` in the UI rather than `0x12bd301a`.

CONFIDENTIALITY ENFORCED AT THE SERVER
Two endpoints serve two projections of the same deal. `/api/deal` (buyer and
supplier) carries the amendment terms those counterparties already hold.
`/api/deal/public` (auditor) is built from named public fields only — the
private keys are not hidden by the client, they are never serialised. A test
asserts this with high-entropy sentinel values (a naive substring check gave a
false positive against a millisecond timestamp, which is why the sentinels are
12 digits), and separately asserts the party view DOES carry them. The auditor
component adds defence in depth by destructuring only named fields — never a
spread, never JSON.stringify.

PROVING THE REPLAY DEFENCE PROPERLY
Re-running the evaluator on an already-settled delivery just returns
ALREADY_CONSUMED, which proves the evaluator works but not the contract. So the
demo also does a forged replay: it resubmits the exact report that already paid,
with a fresh nonce, so the consumer's nonce check cannot catch it. The escrow
reverts. That is the proof that the guarantee lives in the contract, not in
bookkeeping.

MONEY IS NEVER A FLOAT
Every amount is an integer count of minor units carried as a decimal string
across JSON and parsed to bigint at the evaluator boundary. The UI divides by
100 for display only.

BEYOND THE UI
The same capabilities ship as a typed SDK, an `npx` CLI and an MCP server, all
wrapping one client so there is no second implementation to drift. Payment
arithmetic, signatures and authorisation stay entirely outside model control.

TESTING AND DEPLOYMENT
71 tests: 33 Foundry (unit, integration, 128k-call stateful fuzz invariants),
plus deterministic evaluator vectors, ERP contract tests, a real-anvil SDK
end-to-end settlement + replay rejection, and the full browser flow driven
against a devnet. GitHub Actions runs all of them with Foundry installed.

A hosted path exists: a second runtime mode connects to Sepolia instead of
spawning anvil, with off-chain state in Supabase (RLS enabled with zero
policies, so only the service-role key reaches the tables) and the ERP fixture
re-served at Frappe's real path so the client stays unmodified. Mode is derived
from configuration rather than a flag, so a half-configured deployment lists
each missing variable by name instead of looking like it works.

WHAT WE DROPPED
ENSv2 was a candidate third integration. ENS's own docs state the Enhanced
Access Control interfaces are "not yet final", and we could not independently
verify the role methods are live against the published Sepolia addresses. Rather
than ship a cosmetic integration for a logo, we documented the exclusion and
shipped two sponsors properly.
auto_summary: A TypeScript and Solidity system verifies amended purchase-order terms and settles escrowed payments exactly once from ERP-backed delivery confirmations.
